raw_comment:
I run cross country and track where head injuries almost never occur, so looking at this graph was a little bit disturbing. I could never imagine playing a sport that involved a huge chance of being severely hurt. If I had kids, I would never want them doing a sport where high risk of injury was a part of the game. Damage to someone’s brain is nothing to take lightly, and football is the number one contender, by far. 

Ankle, knee and hand injuries also occur in football players much more than any other sport. But truly, these seem insignificant compared to irreversible head injuries. Your hand can heal and your ankle can get wrapped in a cast, but you only get one brain and its healing process is very different than other body parts. 

I hope football players and coaches start to realize the danger and long term effects of damaging teen’s bodies like that.

raw_comment:
“Hard hitters"
The first thing I noticed about this graph is that football, hockey, and wrestling all have the most injuries, which was expected. But why so many head injuries, and why are there any in the first place? The head is easily the worst place to be damaged, as it can lead to concussions and other issues in the future. I think the coaches need to realize that the boys on the team are still kids, and need to play in safer conditions with more protective gear. 
I also wonder why football was the most dangerous sport when you would expect hockey and wrestling to be the same, or even worse. A reason for this may be that football is just too aggressive, and I think they should cut back on the amount of rough contact they make with each other.

raw_comment: The infographic illustrates the variation in the injuries students sustain across different sports. The author used different sized circles overlayed on top of specific body areas to highlight the number of specific injuries for a particular sport in a sample of 10,000 students. We can conclude from the infographic that football is associated with more frequent injuries, especially head, hand, knee, and angle injuries. These results are not surprising – football is contact-heavy, and involves collission of heads, pushing, and quick changes of directions, all which correspond to higher rates of injuries. While the results make sense, I am extremely curious on how the 10,000 samples were collected. The region and district in which a student plays is extremely important because different areas have different regulations on contact and perhaps normalize certain forms of contact that other regions do not. Furthermore, blocking between experienced athletes and new athletes would be effective in order to see if there are any differences between the two groups, as new athletes are likely less fit and have higher risks of becoming injured. Regardless, the infographic and study conducted are important in understanding the relationship between high school sports and injuries – it can be used in helping guide parents in what sports their child should play, and in regulating policies of specific sports. I would title it "When Recreation Becomes Injurious."

raw_comment:
Serious Consequences for a Fun Game 
Football is without a doubt the most popular high school sport. It’s the focus of countless movies, it can get students scholarships, and for a select few, it could become a career. But let’s back up a little, because very few high school football players will ever go pro, and think about what the cost is of playing a contact sport. Every athlete will get injured at some point, it’s a part of the sport. But just because injuries are common, and expected doesn’t mean they aren’t causing some serious damage. 

I noticed that head injuries in football are almost double in any other sport, but with it being America’s most popular sport I wonder why there aren’t more people working to make it safer for those playing it.The short term effects of a concussion are bad enough for high school students, who are too busy to be basically useless for a week or two at school while they’re recovering. That time can set you back! But from what we know, too many head injuries can cause serious effects later in life. Playing football in high school shouldn't mean they should be punished with early memory loss!

image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Bubble chart / proportional symbol chart over body silhouettes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- **Small multiples / faceting by sport**: six side-by-side panels (Football, Hockey, Wrestling, Lacrosse, Soccer, Basketball).  
- Within each panel, bubbles are positioned anatomically on a body outline.  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate side-by-side panels; panel title |
| Body part / injury location (Head, Shoulder, Arm, Hand, Trunk, Thigh, Knee, Lower leg, Ankle) | Categorical/nominal | Spatial position on body silhouette; text labels |
| Injuries per 10,000 competition plays | Quantitative | Bubble/circle size (area); numeric label inside each bubble |

If useful, the body silhouette acts as a background reference for position, not as a separate data variable.

The crazy effects of playing a high school sport    

               I find the results of the graph jarring, to say the least. I notice how many head injuries happen in all the sports, not just football, even though those are the greatest. It makes you wonder if there could be more precautionary measures to prevent head injuries in all sports. I don't play games. But when I was younger, I played soccer but was terrified of the ball hitting me in the face and breaking my glasses. This seems silly now, but looking and the risk of injury in your head still being high in a sport where your not tackling people seems crazy.

I think this would have shown the difference in the roughness you usually see in boys playing sports. I know a lot of injuries when a boy plays a game than if a girl plays the same competition.

raw_comment:
The Wellbeing of Student Athletes
I am a student athlete. I run cross country and track year round, which may not seem like a high impact sport, but it produces many injuries. I know this because I had a stress fracture for almost a year and many of my teammates, both male and female, struggle with the frustration and pain of injuries as well. From my experience, I wonder about the psychological effect on students from being sidelined during their injury and how it varies by sport. I also wonder how the injuries within sports occur. In sports such as football and hockey that are known for high physical impact, it is heavily implied that injuries are caused by the impact. In other sports such as soccer or basketball where there is less contact, I begin to question if the injuries are from overuse (which is what my personal injury was from) or from the contact within the sport. By questioning this, I began to notice how common injuries are for athletes, despite the use of protection such as helmets, shin guards, etc. If injuries are both physically and psychologically taxing for students, who are still adolescents, we should be making sure we are taking all preventative measures possible to ensure that minimal student injuries occur.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all who responded. We had catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs, including “Athletes In Danger!” by Brianna of Hancock, Maryland, and “Use Your Head.  Are These Sports Safe?” by Devyn of Academy of St. Elizabeth, Morristown, New Jersey. Some plays on words like, "Friday Night Hospital Lights" by Mairead of Hoggard High School in Wilmington, NC. Others went a darker route like Kate, Karl, Erika, and Emilie of Eden Prairie High School in Minnesota, with “Keep your head in the game, hopefully.” 

Please continue to post responses and check back tomorrow afternoon, Jan. 30 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

The next graph will be released Friday, Jan. 31, with moderation on Wednesday, February 5. You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to “What's Going On In This Graph?” The topic --  neighborhood racial composition.

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage. Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph.

The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, whose sports injuries are not in these infographics since these are only for high school boys, and Corey Andreasen of Leiden, The Netherlands, who is well represented in this graph.

Headline: Trauma Galore
This graph was very interesting to see. We're already aware of the risk of injury from sports, whether it's through the TV at home or it possibly happening to yourself. But to see it all collected in a data set makes you realize the gravity of these injuries and the possible long term effects it could have on a player.

Growing up hearing stories from my mother about how her brothers used to end up in violent fights after an assumed foul while playing hockey that usually resulted in a staple to head, it was somewhat jarring to see the difference between football and hockey. Perhaps this is the results of new rules being placed in recent years?

Seeing the vast amount of trauma within the ankle as the result of playing football really made me wonder how sports that majorly focus on using the feet like soccer don't have as many injuries. Possibly this is because of the way the balls within the game are handled? I'm not very well-versed in the world of sports so I don't really understand.

Headline: Why so many injuries?
   There are far too many injuries during high school men's sports, especially head injuries. This is what I noticed while observing a graph about how often high school sports players are injured while playing a sport. As a high school lacrosse player, I am appalled by the number of total injuries that occurred. During just 10,000 competition plays, 37 marked injuries took place. I was shocked that there were this many. Even though I know that the sport is very contact-focused, I did not expect a number that high. This number, while it is shocking, is only fourth-highest among popular sports, and it pales in comparison to the number that occur in football. Football causes 34 head injuries every 10,000 plays. raw_comment:
"When does it go too far?"
Looking at this graph, I notice that football has a very high amount of injuries compared to the others. As this does make sense because it is arguably the most contact sport out of the list, it still is ridiculous how many injuries there are. A common similarity I see between all of the sports is that all of them have head injuries. I've had numerous friends have to miss school on many occasions just due to injuries from sports. I'm on the cross country team at Hoggard and have had no injuries because of how they take precautions and try their best for no one to be injured.

I wonder what we could do to make all of these sports safer without taking away the fun aspects of it. Head injuries alone should be our number one concern. You could be a soccer player for high school, make it into college, and then one injury could leave you never being able to play again. With this being said, I would try to come up with ideas to make these sports safer to play while still being able to have a good time.

raw_comment:
"How Many Injuries Will It Take"
How many students have to get injured in order to start taking measures to try and prevent these injuries? When looking at this graph I notice how clear it is that football has an insanely high amount of head injuries. This is unsettling to see because my brother plays football and he's only in middle school. When I was at one of his games, I witnessed a kid on the other team sprain his neck. It was really scary. The ambulance came and he was in the hospital for 2 days. The injuries start even earlier than high school. This many head injuries while their brains are still developing could be dangerous. I definitely don't play football but I myself have had a head injury once before and just that one was enough for me to feel dizzy and have a headache if I read for too long. 
I wonder if there has been any progress in trying to prevent even more head injuries from happening. I find it interesting that basketball has the least amount of injuries even though there seems to be at least one injury during every game.

If useful, the body silhouette acts as a background reference for position, not as a separate data variable.

Headline: "Friday Night Hospital Lights"

When I studied the graph for the first time, I noticed that the most popular American sport, football, has the highest number of injuries sustained per 10,000 competition plays, specifically head injuries.  I knew that football, hockey, and wrestling would have the most injuries even before I read this article due to my prior knowledge.  I have seen many of the Varsity football players at my school in casts and braces for several weeks, but then right back on the field when their doctors said they could, which can cause permanent damage to their bodies.  Also, one of my friends is on the wrestling team and she seriously injured her knee at a match and might not be able to wrestle for the rest of the season.  

I wonder where this data was collected from, whether it all came from one region of the country or from all over.  I wonder this because I have family in Northern Minnesota, and hockey is the most popular sport there by far.  On the other hand, here in North Carolina, hockey isn't very popular at all, but lacrosse is.  If this data is only collected from a certain region of the country, I wonder how much it would differ if it was collected from other regions as well.

Headline: Hungry to Win, How Hungry is Too Hungry?
From this graph I notice that there are many risks associated with playing any sport, especially as a boy, due to their competitive and aggressive nature. Football is most commonly known for its head injuries, the debates on how to make it safer are plentiful. Constant arguing over whether or not to change the rules, the equipment, or even the entire sport to make it safer for kids. Something that needs to be pointed out is that there is risk associated with everything sport you play, it just depends on how comfortable you are with taking those risks. After looking at this graph, I wonder what keeps these boys interested in these sports if there is such a high risk of injury. I guess it could be their high adrenaline levels, their aggressive nature as stated before, or just their hunger to the best. But where is the line between risk and reward? All Injuries add up over time and take a large toll on your body? As an athlete, I’m not against playing sports and getting hurt, it builds character and helps us develop into stronger people, but it’s the ones who push themselves past their threshold that I'm worried about. Sports are good for your health, mentally and physically, for the most part, it’s one of the best ways to release your anger and frustration, and it keeps you in shape but you need to understand when you've overworked yourself.

raw_comment:
Heading: Friday Night Fatalities 
If you take time to study the graph you easily notice the fact the football has the most substantial injuries. The first three don’t surprise me because they are contact sports. What does surprise me is the fact that football has an overwhelming amount of injuries. The worst part is the fact that the head injuries are so high. Football players wear a good amount of protection yet they still rank the highest for injuries. This leads me to ask the question, how protected are they actually. One of my friends from middle school had suffered about three concussions from his time while playing football. He was a quarterback with a lot of potential, but was taken off the team by his mother out of fear, and rightfully so. Before this school year started my friend was debating weather to play football or wrestling. I was relieved to hear he would be joining the wrestling team. I wondered why I was so relieved by what he told me. Then I came to the conclusion that you hear more horror stories about football and all the awful articles about brain injuries and their consequences. I wonder what we can do to make these sports a bit more safer all together.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Bubble chart / proportional symbol chart over body silhouettes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- **Small multiples / faceting by sport**: six side-by-side panels (Football, Hockey, Wrestling, Lacrosse, Soccer, Basketball).  
- Within each panel, bubbles are positioned anatomically on a body outline.  
- No stacking.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate side-by-side panels; panel title |
| Body part / injury location (Head, Shoulder, Arm, Hand, Trunk, Thigh, Knee, Lower leg, Ankle) | Categorical/nominal | Spatial position on body silhouette; text labels |
| Injuries per 10,000 competition plays | Quantitative | Bubble/circle size (area); numeric label inside each bubble |

If useful, the body silhouette acts as a background reference for position, not as a separate data variable.
raw_comment: In this graph, I notice that arguably the most physical sport, football, has the most injuries. These are serious injuries to the head, ankle, knee, etc. that prevent people from competing in the thing they love to do most. I wonder how these injuries impact their life and future career. The graph also shows that different sports have different injuries regarding the human body, like how basketball tends to have many more ankle injuries than hockey while hockey players suffer many more shoulder injuries than basketball players. As an athlete, I know how painful it is not only to have the injury, but to have to suffer with the fact that I cannot compete in the thing I love doing most. So while every athlete is bound to get an injury playing whatever sport they love, it is important to have the safest equipment possible to insure that every child and adult can compete at the highest level possible.

Headline: Love of the game?
  When I look at this graph I immediately notice that majority of the incidents are head injuries. I understand people have dedication and love for whatever sport they may play, but why would you play to the extent of potentially hurting yourself or others?
Do the players ever fathom weather they will get hurt or do they just play until it’s too late to rethink their decisions? I’m not one to understand the wanting to be apart of a sport and play to my hearts’ desire, but I do understand the love of doing something you're passionate about. My passion for music drives me to practice beyond hours of exhaustion, and to never give up on a piece of music, no matter how hard it is. 
  I know the line of hobbies is extremely different, but when I look at this graph a part of me does understand. Even though the game is difficult and may end up suffering from whatever injury, the game itself, and the experience and joy it brings from being apart of it is something you feel you can’t be without. But I wonder, if the injury itself could have been avoided, would the player make the same choice, for the sake of the game?

raw_comment:
I have noticed a few things about this graph. It’s interesting how hockey has more injuries than wrestling, despite wrestling having direct person to person contact. Another piece of information also surprised me is that basketball has more ankle injuries than most of the sports listed such as soccer and hockey where I would think ankle injuries would be much more prominent. Some things are to be expected, such as soccer having less injuries than football and hockey.
       What has my interest piqued, is that over the years I know that many people have been trying to improve and have focused on making head injuries safer for football. I think I’m just surprised that such a big sport in America would have so much more injuries statistically even with how much attention it has gotten. Maybe it already has improved, we would need an earlier chart to tell. If so, I hope the numbers continue to decline. Headline: Put Ice On It 
At first glance, I noticed a commonality between sports were head injuries. I thought that football,lacrosse and hockey would have the most overall injuries because of how physical the sports are. I was surprised however when I saw that wrestling was listed above lacrosse for certain injuries such as head and arms. I play basketball and through that I have had a concussion and a dislocated finger. Sitting out was no fun and when I was playing again I still felt like I was gonna get hurt again.  When I watch friends of mine that play these sports come away with major or minor injuries it makes me wonder how and when things will change so the players feel more protected and can play aggressively but safe. Myself, like any other sports lover, want to watch a good game that is lively and competitive. However, it becomes unbearable to watch when players have to be carted off the fields or courts. As sports takes a front seat in more people's lives, it's an important  job to take care of our athletes.
